newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Melbourne airport eyes Sydney's Olympic business.
newsitem.headline: Melbourne airport eyes Sydney's Olympic business.

text.p: The consortium that owns Melbourne international airport, Asia Pacific Airports (APA), said on Wednesday the airport would market itself as an alternative to Sydney airport during the 2000 Olympic Games.

"I question Sydney airport's capacity to handle the numbers of international flights during the period of the Games," APA's chief executive Andrew Jurenko told a luncheon hosted by the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia (CEDA).
"We believe there is a prime opportunity for Melbourne to be marketing itself as an alternative and preferable route in and out of the Olympic city," Jurenko said.
Jurenko said APA would be holding discussions with the state government of Victoria and the airlines on how this option could be best developed and marketed.
The Federal government sold Melbourne airport to APA in May for A$1.307 billion as a part of phase one of its airport privatisation program which also saw the sale of the Brisbane and Perth airports.
The government has said it will not sell Sydney international airport, Australia's largest, until after aircraft noise problems surrounding the operation are resolved.

"The issue of the second (proposed Sydney international) airport has yet to be resolved but I have no doubt that if the second airport becomes part of the privatisation package, then Sydney would not be up for sale until well after the year 2000," Jurenko said.
If this situation eventuated Melbourne airport would have a significant head start in developing and marketing its facilities, he said.
Sydney was adequately serviced in terms of its airport to operate for another twenty years, Jurenko said.
"I see no financial logic in including the second airport in the sale of Sydney airport - a second airport will turn a potential financial plus to government into a financial nightmare," he said.

He said it was worth noting that London's Heathrow airport could handle 80 million passengers a year with two runways, Gatwick with one runway could handle up to 40 million but Sydney with three runways had less than 20 million passengers a year. "The main problem of a second city airport is that airlines do not like split operations. They result in vastly increased operating costs," Jurenko said.
He also said given the large number of aviation developments around Sydney airport it was difficult to believe a second major airport would be viable for many years.

The APA group comprises British airport operator, BAA Plc with an initial 25.1 percent stake, insurance and funds group AMP Society with 49.9 percent and Sydney-based funds manager, Deutsche Bank AG's Axiom, with 25 percent.
BAA's stake would fall to 15.1 percent if a proposed fourth partner, Melbourne-based Hastings Fund Management, exercised an option to take a 10 percent interest.
